The Coumarou, Myloplus rhomboidalis, is a freshwater characiform fish native to the rivers of the Guiana Shield. Field studies have documented that females reach sexual maturity and are capable of spawning at a total length of 25 cm [Lp = 25 cm], a size that corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis and gonadal recrudescence. At this stage of reproductive activation, individuals typically weigh approximately 287 grams [Wwp = approximately 287 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions for the species. The maximum standard length ever recorded for this species is 40.5 cm [Li = 40.5 cm], a size observed in only the oldest and largest individuals collected during extensive surveys. The calculated ultimate wet weight, based on a length-weight regression for the genus, is 5000 grams [Wwi = 5000 grams], a value that likely overestimates the true asymptotic mass; field records of the largest individuals rarely exceed 1200 grams, suggesting that the allometric model may not capture the species' true growth curve. These morphological benchmarks provide a foundation for understanding the life history strategy of this serrasalmid fish, which occupies a specialized niche in neotropical floodplain ecosystems.


The early life stages of Coumarou are characterized by rapid development, particularly under stable thermal conditions. At a constant water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the yolk-sac larva absorbs its endogenous reserves and commences exogenous feeding approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days] after fertilization, marking the transition from a lecithotrophic to an exotrophic mode of nutrition. Hatchlings emerge from the adhesive demersal eggs at a remarkably small size; the wet weight at birth is a mere 0.0115 grams [Wwb = 0.0115 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of approximately 2.8 mm for a related congener. This low initial mass reflects the minimal yolk reserves allocated to each offspring, a common trait among characiform fishes that produce numerous, small pelagic larvae. The early onset of feeding is critical for survival, as the tiny larvae must quickly locate planktonic prey to sustain their rapid growth trajectory through the flexion and postflexion larval stages.


Reproductive output in Coumarou has been characterized through both field observations and modeling approaches based on length-fecundity relationships for serrasalmids. Under the environmental conditions typical of its native range, at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], individual females achieve a maximum annual reproductive rate that can be understood by examining their fecundity and spawning frequency. A female at the ultimate length produces approximately 307,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 307,000 eggs per spawning event], a number derived from the allometric scaling of fecundity with body size. These spawnings occur roughly three times per year [F_R_i = roughly three times per year], a pattern consistent with the iteroparous strategy observed in related Myleus species during the extended wet season. This combined reproductive effort represents a considerable investment, with a large female capable of releasing well over 900,000 eggs annually to maximize recruitment success in a variable floodplain environment. This equates to a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 921,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 921,000 eggs per year].


Longevity and lifespan estimates for Coumarou suggest a moderately extended life for a fish of its body size. The maximum lifespan recorded under conditions approximating its natural thermal regime, at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], is approximately 2190 days [am = approximately 2190 days], a duration of about six years that places it among the longer-lived members of its genus. This relatively protracted lifespan is likely an adaptation to the seasonal and interannual variability of the neotropical river systems it inhabits, where favorable spawning conditions may not materialize every year. The ability to survive and reproduce across multiple breeding seasons allows the species to buffer against periodic recruitment failures. This life history strategy contrasts with that of smaller, more short-lived characiforms, which tend to exhibit higher annual mortality but earlier maturity and more frequent spawning events within a compressed adult lifespan.


Comparative studies within the Serrasalmidae reveal that Coumarou occupies an intermediate position on the fast-slow life history continuum. This species attains its ultimate standard length of 40.5 cm [Li = 40.5 cm] after several years of growth, and the onset of puberty at 25 cm [Lp = 25 cm] represents a significant life-history transition, after which energy allocation shifts towards reproduction while somatic growth continues. The relatively high wet weight at puberty of 287 grams [Wwp = 287 grams] relative to its ultimate wet weight of 5000 grams [Wwi = 5000 grams] indicates that a disproportionate amount of growth occurs after sexual maturation—a pattern common in fishes that continue to invest in somatic growth while reproducing. This indeterminate growth strategy enables the species to increase fecundity with age, as larger, older females contribute disproportionately to the next generation through higher per-spawn egg production.
